rationale: A wins because it has better editorial self-control: it turns the same facts into targetable shapes and refuses the unsupported temptation, "Live shopping isn't dead in America after all." B has two useful angles, then strolls into fabrication with "Whatnot is betting US shoppers behave like Asia's — the data so far says they don't." That headline asserts data the prompt never gave; that's not contrarian, that's a lawsuit wearing better shoes.
gaps_in_A: "card sellers built the $3B" is not in the update. We know Whatnot started with cards and collectibles; we do not know cards generated or built the $3B.
"Those categories have established marketplaces" is plausible, but the set needs named incumbents or sourced category context before making the competition angle carry real conflict.
"find-journalists" is a little premature as the next step. Before list-building, the founder still needs to verify GMV vs. revenue, timeframe, category split, and the Asia source.
gaps_in_B: "the data so far says they don't" invents a conclusion. The update says Asia is larger; it does not provide US-vs-Asia behavior data.
"long-running, repeatedly-failed attempts to make Western live shopping work" is outside the supplied facts. That may be true in the world, but it was not in the brief.
"US-born platform" is not supplied, and "first hard data point that the format scales past collectors" overclaims because the $3B may still be mostly collectibles.
The first and third angles are too close: both orbit US-vs-Asia live-commerce adoption, one hopeful and one skeptical. That is a mood change, not a clean structural split.
